open-question.question: `CLAUDE.md` records the design decisions a later editor must not undo, often by naming a retired form with a ban on restoring it. Does it gain such an entry for the hard cut, naming the retired forms (the `milestones/` container, the `--milestone` flag, the `Milestone-definition:` and `Milestone-finish:` markers, `/migrate-milestones`) as never to be accepted or read again, which keeps the old word in the file by decision, or does it describe only the new shape?
open-question.recommendation: One entry stating that the plugin answers to its current names only, with no alias, no second discovery pattern, and no migration, and on what ground, already rules every retired form out, so naming them would add only a search hit at the price of the old word standing in the file for good; the entry is needed because this work's own record ends as a finish commit the renamed tool never prints, and it carries the bootstrap's recorded replacement of an older workflow section as its stated exception.
open-question.alternative: `CLAUDE.md` gains one dedicated entry for the hard cut, written only in the new vocabulary and naming no retired form. It states the rule positively: the plugin answers to its current names only, through one flag, one discovery pattern (`**/mission_*/requirements.md`), and one finish marker. There is no alias and no second pattern, the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, and no migration is shipped. It gives the low-adoption ground as the reason. The decision and its reason are recorded where later editors look for what must not be undone, and the file adds no occurrence of the old word, so the hard cut adds nothing to the residue the sibling completeness bar has to account for. A ban that names nothing cannot be found by searching for the thing it bans. An editor working from a bug report that quotes `--milestone` or `Milestone-finish:` has to recognise for themselves that "one flag, no alias" covers it, which is weaker protection than the file gives every other retired form.

`CLAUDE.md` gains one dedicated invariant entry for the hard cut. It names each retired form literally (the `milestones/` container and its `**/milestones/*/requirements.md` pattern, the `--milestone` flag, the `Milestone-definition:` and `Milestone-finish:` markers, `/migrate-milestones`) and bans accepting, reading, or restoring any of them, with no alias, no second discovery pattern, and no migration. It records that the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, gives the one ground the draft records (Cairn was not widely adopted), and takes the place of the `migrate-milestones` invariant, which goes with its skill. The old word stays in that entry by decision. It follows the file's own pattern for retired forms: the seven "must not be restored" bans and the pre-split entry name what they retire. An editor who greps for `--milestone` or `Milestone-finish:` because a user reports an old project finds the ban and its reason in one place, so a well-meant alias or compatibility reader is stopped before it is written. It keeps the old word in `CLAUDE.md` permanently, as residue that has to be listed and told apart from a leftover however the sibling rename-completeness bar is set. The named forms can also read as live vocabulary to a runner that skims the file.

`CLAUDE.md` gains one dedicated entry that names the retired forms literally, as the first option does. It records the cut as a stated limit of the current design rather than a permanent ban: the renamed plugin accepts and reads none of the old forms and promises no reader or migration, the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, and a later milestone may add an upgrade path if adoption shows the need, in the way the existing `Tasklist-completion:` note leaves its commits unread "with no later reader promised". The old word stays in that entry by decision. It keeps the reason and the named forms findable in one place without closing a door the low-adoption ground may not justify closing for good. A later migration, if one is ever wanted, is then a revision of a recorded limit, not the reversal of a ban. A limit invites the very compatibility work the goal rules out: an editor reading "may add" can treat an alias or a dual reader as an open gap and fill it piecemeal. It also keeps the old word in the file as listed residue, the same cost as the first option.

No dedicated entry. Each existing invariant that owns a site the cut touches gains one clause naming the retired form it dropped and banning its return: the resolution invariant names the dropped `--milestone` flag, the read-only tool's invariant names the old discovery pattern and the `Milestone-finish:` marker and records that the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, the definition invariant names the `milestones/` container and `Milestone-definition:`, and the commit invariant notes that `/migrate-milestones` and its `--date` caller are gone. The old word stays in each of those clauses by decision. Each ban sits where an editor changing that site already reads, as the read-only tool's invariant already notes its own record limit beside the query it limits, so it protects the edit most likely to bring a form back. The old word is scattered across several entries instead of standing in one, which makes the residue harder to list and check. The single reason for the cut is either repeated at each site or stated nowhere whole.

No dedicated entry, and no retired form named. Each invariant that owns an affected site states its own rule in the new vocabulary with an exclusive "only": the resolution invariant says only `--mission` is recognised, the read-only tool's invariant says it reads `Mission-finish:` subjects and the one `mission_*` pattern only and that the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, and the definition invariant says the mission stands directly in its scope with no container. The cut is never described as a cut. The limits are stated where they apply and are checkable against each tool's contract, and `CLAUDE.md` gains no occurrence of the old word anywhere. Nothing records that a compatibility path was weighed and refused, or why. An "only" reads as a description of today rather than a decision, so a later alias or migration looks like an extension, not an undoing, and grepping for an old name finds nothing.

`CLAUDE.md` records nothing of the hard cut: no entry, no clause, and no exclusive wording beyond describing the new shape as it is. The `migrate-milestones` invariant and every other mention of the old forms are removed, and the decision is recorded only in this milestone's `## Decisions`, in `ideas/gurita.md`, and in whatever the documentation and help text say about where the record starts. This is permanent, not a postponement. The file stays a description of the plugin as it is, with no old word and nothing extra for the completeness bar to list. A hard cut on a little-adopted plugin arguably needs no guard, since there are few users whose reports would prompt a compatibility path. The file whose job is to stop a later editor undoing a design decision would be silent on one of the largest decisions this release makes. The places it would live instead are weak: `ideas/` drafts may be revised or dropped, and this milestone's decisions survive only at its finish commit's parent, which `summary` and `show` reach only if the sibling own-finish question makes that commit a `Mission-finish:` one.

open-question.question: The principle store moves from `milestones/answer_decision_principles.md` to `answer_decision_principles.md` at the project root, and the renamed recommendation procedure and capture skill name only the new path. A store an existing project holds at the old path is therefore read by nothing after the upgrade: its recommendations lose every confirmed principle without any sign, and its next capture starts a new store at the root. What is done for such a store: does the bootstrap move it, as it already replaces an older workflow section; does the documentation this work rewrites tell the project to move the file by hand; or is it left unmentioned?
open-question.recommendation: The recorded bootstrap decision already makes that skill the one run that brings an existing project's guidance to the new form, and a project holding a store at the old path holds the old section too, so the same run and commit carry its confirmed principles to the root with no step for a person to remember; left to capture, to a report, or to the docs, recommendations lose them without sign in the meantime, and a fallback read would keep an old path read for good.
open-question.alternative: The bootstrap carries the old store over as part of the pass that replaces an older workflow section: when `milestones/answer_decision_principles.md` stands and `answer_decision_principles.md` at the root does not, it moves the file to the root unchanged and commits both paths with the context file in its one `Workflow-bootstrap: missions` commit; when both stand, or only the new one does, it moves nothing. The old path is named literally in the bootstrap skill, beside the old heading it already names by decision, and in `core/shared/workflow-guidance.md` only if its third case describes the move. The recommendation procedure and the capture skill name only the new path, and the docs describe the move as part of what the bootstrap does. The one upgrade step a project already takes under the recorded bootstrap decision also carries its confirmed principles across, so no recommendation loses them and no capture starts a second store, with nothing for a person to remember and the fix landing in a reviewable commit. It protects only a project that re-runs the bootstrap at the upgrade, which nothing requires and which the skill describes as a once-per-project step, and it widens a skill whose whole duty is the context file into a second path and a move, keeping the old path in runtime prose and adding a both-stand case to state.

The capture skill, the store's sole writer, moves it: at its start, when the old-path store stands and the root one does not, it moves the file to the root and uses it as the baseline, the move riding in the same `Principle-capture:` commit as the rewrite (and on a rejected or nothing-captured run, restoring the store where it stood). The old path is named literally in the capture skill only. The bootstrap and the recommendation procedure are unchanged and name only the new path, and the docs describe the move in the capture entry. The store's location stays owned by the one skill that writes it, and the split-store damage, a new root store started beside an orphaned old one, cannot happen, since the first capture after the upgrade carries every confirmed principle forward. Every recommendation made between the upgrade and the next capture still reads no store and loses its principles without sign, and capture's already intricate snapshot, rejection, and no-op paths gain a move to undo, with the old path kept in runtime prose.

No plugin step moves the file; the two readers detect it and say so. The capture skill, when the old-path store stands and the root one does not, stops before any write on a fixed line of its own, with the `git mv` that moves it beneath, so no second store is started; the recommendation procedure, finding no root store and the old-path one standing, has its runner report that in its advisory, naming the same move. Both name the old path literally to test for it and never read its contents, a new fixed-line row and its test case are added, and the docs name only the new path. The loss is never silent at either reader, while the plugin itself moves and reads nothing of the old form, so the hard cut holds for the content and the person upgrading decides when the move is made. It adds old-path probes and new reporting to two runtime sites, one of them a shared procedure also followed by `discuss-open-question`, and a fixed line that exists only for an upgrade, and the principles stay unread until a person acts on the report.

The store is never moved by anything: the recommendation procedure reads it at the root when it stands there and at `milestones/answer_decision_principles.md` otherwise, and the capture skill rewrites whichever of the two holds it, creating it at the root only when neither does. Both name both paths literally in their prose and commands, this repository's own store still moving to the root as already decided, and the docs state the old path as accepted. An existing project loses nothing and does nothing at the upgrade, with no move, no report, and no step that has to be run at the right moment. It keeps a read of an old-form path in runtime permanently, against the goal's hard cut in which nothing of the old vocabulary is accepted or read, and doubles every store path in the capture skill's guard, snapshot, diff, and restore commands for as long as the plugin lives.

No runtime change: the recommendation procedure and the capture skill name only the new path. The documentation this work rewrites, the capture entry of `docs/skill-reference.md` and the learning-loop paragraph of `docs/workflow.md`, states that a store a project holds at `milestones/answer_decision_principles.md` is read by nothing after the upgrade and is moved by hand to `answer_decision_principles.md` at the root, with the `git mv` that does it. The project is told exactly what to do in the places that describe the store, at the cost of one sentence in each and no runtime code, fixed line, or old-path probe. A project that does not read the docs at the upgrade still loses its principles without sign, and the old path enters the rewritten docs by decision; whether the docs carry upgrade guidance at all is the axis the Upgrade guidance placement question owns, so this option holds only where that question lets the docs say what a project does at the upgrade.

Nothing is done for an old-path store in this work: no runtime step moves, reads, or detects it, and the docs this work rewrites name only the new root path, any word to existing projects being left to the release notes the plugin rename's work writes, or to none. The hard cut stays whole, with no old path anywhere in runtime prose or the rewritten docs and no code or fixed line that exists only for an upgrade, and the work stays the rename it set out to be. An upgraded project's recommendations silently stop weighing every confirmed principle, and its next capture starts a fresh root store beside the orphaned one, a split nobody is told about, unless the plugin rename's release notes happen to cover it.
